## ABSTRACT

RESEARCH PAPER: Development and Application of a High Throughput Assay System for

the Detection of Rieske Dioxygenase Activity

STUDENT: Cristina Preston-Herrera

DEGREE: Master of Arts

COLLEGE: Science and Humanities

DATE: May 2021

PAGES: 32

The chemical industry currently accounts for 14% of all greenhouse gas emissions and is

projected to become the largest global consumer of oil by 2030. In the Ball State Laboratory for

Biocatalysis Research, we strive to address this problem through the development and application

of novel enzymatic catalysts. Enzymatic catalysts are environmentally benign because they can be

used in aqueous solutions and are fully biodegradable. As such, they can play a role in eliminating

the need for petroleum-based solvents and toxic heavy-metal catalysts in the production of fine

chemicals.

Rieske dioxygenases (RDO) are a class of enzymes known for their ability to perform the

cis-dihydroxylation of aromatic compounds. They have been widely applied in synthetic chemistry

due to their ability to provide enantiopure metabolites that can be used in the synthesis of high-

value compounds. Yet, the utility of these enzymes has been limited by their substrate scope and

strict selectivity.

Here, we seek to develop novel RDO catalysts with improved or expanded reactivity

through directed evolution. In order to detect the relative cis-dihydroxylation activity of engineered

Rieske dioxygenase variants, a novel high throughput assay system for the detection of their cis-


<!-- Page 3 -->

diol metabolites was developed. Here, the cis-diol metabolites produced by active dioxygenases

in aqueous fermentation broths are oxidized using sodium (meta)periodate to produce diene-

dialdehydes. These dialdehydes are then conjugated with a reactive fluorescent probe to give a

strong, concentration-dependent fluorescent signal. In this way, this metaperiodate fluorescein cis-

diol assay (MPFCD) detects the relative activity of RDOs with different aromatic substrates. This

novel high throughput assay system has allowed for the activity of rationally engineered Rieske

dioxygenase variants, produced through saturation mutagenesis, to be determined, and for the

identification of variants that demonstrate significantly altered reactivity profiles in comparison to

the parent enzyme.

## Introduction

Thanks to an increase in research in the field of enzyme engineering, a framework for

expanding and improving the reactivity of existing natural enzymes has been developed. Enzymes

are sophisticated proteins that can take materials from the environment and convert them to a

product with high selectivity and efficiency under mild and environmentally benign conditions.1

Traditional synthetic chemistry methodology relies heavily on the use of petroleum based solvents,

toxic reagents, and precious metals that can generate unwanted side products.1 To abate the

environmental impact of the chemical industry, biocatalysis has increasingly been employed  in

synthetic chemistry.

One of the first reports of biocatalysis came in 1886 by A. J. Brown, where Acinetobacter

cells were used to convert ethanol to acetic acid and mannitol to fructose.2 By the 1990s, enzymes

were widely used by industrial processes for the production of chiral compounds needed for the

synthesis of pharmaceuticals, fragrances and plant protecting agents.3

In 1968, Professor David Gibson discovered a class of enzymes now known to commonly

exist in soil bacteria, the Rieske dioxygenases.4 This class of enzymes catalyze the first step in the

metabolic pathway responsible for the degradation of many anthropogenic aromatic pollutants

such as toluene through oxidative dearomatization (Figure 1).5

*Figure 1: Metabolic pathway responsible for the degradation of aromatic substrates with mutant/transgenic strains compared to wild strain.*


<!-- Page 5 -->


4

Dr. Gibson soon realized that bacteria expressing Rieske dioxygenases could be used to

generate cis-diol metabolites, which could be useful as starting material for synthesis owing to

their high enantiopurity and diverse reactivity.6, 7 Therefore, Dr. Gibson created a mutant bacterial

strain, P. putida 39D, that lacks the enzymes responsible for further metabolizing the cis-diols to

catechols; and later a transgenic E.coli strain (JM109 (pDTG601A)) that was deficient in the

enzymes responsible for the further degradation of these metabolites, to allow for the accumulation

of these diene-diol metabolites in fermentation cultures (Figure 1).8, 9 Since Dr. Gibson’s

discovery of toluene dioxygenase, much research has been done on Rieske dioxygenases. This

class of enzymes are the only class known to perform the dihydroxylation of aromatic substrates

to give the corresponding diene cis-diols.10 In 2009, Friemann et al. published the structure of

toluene dioxygenase (Figure 2).11

*Figure 2: Structure of ferredoxin (todB) and oxygenase (todC1C2) enzyme system. Cluster binding domain of ferredoxin is shown in gray, oxygenase alpha unit shown in green, yellow and red.*


<!-- Page 6 -->


5

The four components of the toluene dioxygenase system are reductaseTOL (todA),

ferredoxinTOL (todB), and two terminal subunits of the dioxygenase iron sulfur protein, ISPTOL

(todC1C2).9 Here, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH) transfers electrons via flavin

adenine dinucleotide (FAD) in the reductase, to the ferredoxin where electrons are then shuttled to

the terminal dioxygenase via the Rieske-type [2Fe-2S] center (Figure 3A).11, 12 Electrons from the

iron-sulfur cluster are transferred to another Rieske center in the oxygenase unit where these

electrons are moved to the mononuclear iron coordinated by two histidine residues and one

aspartate.11 The enantioselective dihydroxylation of aromatic compounds is coordinated by the

“side-on” binding of oxygen to iron (Figure 3B).11

The large-scale production of Rieske dioxygenase metabolites has allowed for the

development of new synthetic avenues for the production of valuable compounds such as, pinitol,

anti-cancer agents, opiate analgesics and many others (Figure 4).13-15

*Figure 3: A) Electron transport scheme for Rieske dioxygenases; B) Mechanism of oxygenase catalyzed dihydroxylation of aromatic compounds.*


<!-- Page 7 -->


6

Despite these diverse applications, the utility of Rieske dioxygenases remains limited by

their substrate scope and strict selectivity in terms of size, sterics, and electrostatic potential of

potential substrates.16-19 To overcome these limitations, methods to alter the reactivity of TDO by

saturated/random mutagenesis have been investigated and have led to increase production in

metabolites, and changes in chemo/enantioselectivity of the enzyme (Figure 5). 17, 20-23

However, to enable truly large-scale enzyme engineering efforts, an approachable and high

throughput screening method for the detection of Rieske dioxygenase activity, both in the native

enzymes and in the engineered variants, is required. Existing methods for Rieske dioxygenase

*Figure 5: Examples of TDO variants produced via synthetic biology and active site targeted mutagenesis.17, 23*

mutant screening, are limited to the colorimetric indigo assay, oxygen electrode-based screening

platforms, Flow-Injection Analysis (FIA) techniques, liquid/gas chromatography and the

colorimetric Gibbs assay.24 While these screening methods are effective, in some cases they

provide little insight into the relative metabolite production of variant enzymes or substrate scope,

and in other cases they can require expensive/sensitive equipment which limit the amount of

variants that can be screened.24 For these reasons, the MPFCD assay system is a promising

screening method to detect variants with novel reactivity; this assay system can be coupled with

established methods for the generation of mutant enzyme libraries to facilitate the large-scale

screening of Rieske dioxygenase variants for new or improved reactivity.

## Results and Discussion

Development of MPFCD Assay

In order to establish a program in the engineering of improved Rieske dioxygenase

variants, an approachable and high throughput assay system for the detection of Rieske

dioxygenase activity was required. There is strong literature precent for the facile detection of

aldehyde-bearing metabolites produced by enzymes in fermentation cultures.25, 26

Fluoresceinamine has been used to generate a strong, detectable fluorescent response in the

presence of aldehyde metabolites generated by dehydrogenase enzymes from Gluconobacter

oxydans in aqueous media.25 The parent structure of fluoresceinamine is weakly fluorescent due

to its tendency for intramolecular self-quenching, but fluoresceinamine can have a strong

fluorescent signal when the amine functional group is conjugated to an aldehyde in the form of an

imine.25 Once fluoresceinamine is conjugated to an aldehyde, the electrons from the amine will no


<!-- Page 9 -->


8

longer contribute to the electron rich aromatic ring of fluorescein, which will significantly increase

the fluorescence of the fluorescein structure.25, 27 This fluorescence response of fluoresceinamine

in the presence of aldehydes in aqueous media has further been shown to be concentration-

dependent, which enables this reaction to be used to quantify the amount of aldehyde metabolite

present in a sample.25 With this knowledge, the well-known reaction of periodate with cis vicinal

diols to produce aldehydes was employed to perform the oxidative cleavage of the cis-diol

metabolites produced by Rieske dioxygenases.28 This conversion of the cis-diol metabolites to

dialdehydes with sodium periodate was then used in combination with conjugation of the resultant

dialdehydes with the fluoresceinamine probe (Figure 6A). Initial studies demonstrated that these

combined reactions were effective in generating a concentration-dependent fluorescent response

in the presence of the cis-diol metabolites (Figure 6B).

*Figure 6: A) Oxidation of cis-diol metabolites to corresponding dialdehyde coupled with conjugation to the fluorescent probe fluoresceinamine; B) Concentration-dependent fluorescent response of the assay to the presence of cis-diol metabolites.*

After the initial studies confirmed the utility of our assay system in detecting the presence

of cis-diol metabolites, optimization studies were undertaken to maximize the sensitivity of this

assay system. These optimization studies varied the final concentration of sodium metaperiodate

(NaIO4), the final concentration of fluoresceinamine, the final pH of the assay media, and the

buffer media components utilized in the assay. To conduct these experiments, a 1 L-scale

biotransformation of toluene was performed using E. coli (JM109 (pDTG601A)) expressing

toluene dioxygenase to provide a sufficient amount of the corresponding cis-diol metabolite to

facilitate the optimization studies.9 This metabolite, (1S,2R)-3-methylcyclohexa-3,5-diene-1,2-

diol, was used to conduct all optimization studies. The fluorescence response of the assay system

with varied concentrations of NaIO4 and fluoresceinamine were studied in a HEPES buffered

solution (0.1M) at pH 7.2. Here it was observed that large excess of sodium metaperiodate (10-50

fold excess) gave the strongest fluorescence response (Figure 7A). Final concentration of

fluoresceinamine at 0.1 mM gave optimal fluorescence response (Figure 7B), which confirmed

reports from a previous study.25


<!-- Page 11 -->


10

With preliminary data on the amount of oxidizing agent and fluorescent probe, studies

using various buffer systems were performed using 0.1M of HEPES (N-(2-

Hydroxyethyl)piperazine-N′-(2-ethanesulfonic acid)), TRIS (2-Amino-2-(hydroxymethyl)-1,3-

propanediol), PIPES (1,4-Piperazinediethanesulfonic acid) and potassium phosphate. From these

studies it was observed that HEPES gave the greatest fluorescence response while TRIS gave the

weakest (Figure 8A). The low response observed in the TRIS buffer can be explained by the three

hydroxyl moieties of TRIS which can coordinate with sodium metaperiodate and limit the

reactivity of the periodate in oxidizing the cis-diol.29 Having identified HEPES as the best-

performing buffer system, pH studies were conducted to determine what pH gives the best

*Figure 7: Assay optimization studies; A) Fluorescence response of the assay with varied concentrations of sodium metaperiodate (0.1M HEPES, pH 7.2, 0.1M of fluoresceinamine); B) Fluorescence response of the assay with varied concentrations of fluoresceinamine (0.1M HEPES, pH 7.2, 10 mM sodium metaperiodate).*

11

reactivity within the HEPES buffering range.29, 30 From these studies, it was observed that lower

pH levels gave a stronger fluorescence response (Figure 8B). This can be explained because acid

is required for the formation of the imine. This acid catalyzed imine formation is required for the

conjugation of the fluorescent dialdehyde-probe.31 Fluorescein derivatives are known to form

various ionic equilibria, with the monoanionic (pKa ~6.7) and dianion species being the only

known derivatives known to show fluorescence.32-34 This indicated that the increase in

fluorescence at lower pH levels was a result of the increase formation of fluoresceinamine-

dialdehyde conjugate  rather than a result of improved fluorescence output for the protonated

conjugate. These pH studies found that the optimal balance between increased imine formation

and the reduced fluorescence of the protonated conjugate to be at pH ~6.5 (Figure 9). With data

on the best conditions for optimal fluorescence response confirmed, a time-course study was

conducted to determine the time required to produce the maximal fluorescence response. From

this study, it was noted that increased fluorescence was observed over extended reaction times

(Figure 8C). Based on this data, the assay reaction time was henceforth standardized at five hours.

To determine the sensitive of this assay system, lower concentrations of cis-diol metabolites were

tested under the optimized assay conditions, which showed that this MPFCD assay could produce

a significant fluorescence response with concentrations of cis-diol as low as 10 µM (Figure 8D).

Detection of Metabolites Produced by Respiring Cells

In a similar fashion to how Dr. David Gibson developed a vector for the transgenic

expression of the genes of toluene dioxygenase by laboratory E. coli strains, our next goal was to

develop a more modern vector for the overexpression of the toluene dioxygenase genes. It was

determined that development of such a vector, with the capability to increase the amount of protein

produced by our expression E. coli strains in fermentation cultures, would result in an increase in

the dihydroxylation of aromatic compounds. This increase in metabolite production could be

essential for the MPFCD assay to detect the often small perturbations in activity caused by the

introduction of mutations into the toluene dioxygenase genes. To accomplish this goal, the existing

pDTG601A vector carrying the todC1C2BA enzyme cassette was used for cloning. The todC2AB

(non-catalytic) components of TDO were cloned into the MCS-2 site of pCDF-Duet-1, a vector

template selected for its two available multiple cloning sites, to yield the plasmid pCP-01. This

plasmid, lacking the catalytic dioxygenase activity, was then used as a negative control in all

subsequent dihydroxylation experiments. The catalytic dioxygenase subunit (todC1) was then

cloned into the MCS-1 site of the pCP-01 vector to afford the plasmid pCP-02. The visual indigo

assay demonstrated that this novel pCP-02 vector was catalytically active.24 The amount of cis-

diol metabolites produced by cells expressing pCP-02 was compared to the metabolite production

by cells expressing the existing system (pDTG601A) using the MPFCD assay. This study

demonstrated significantly increased metabolites production from the pCP-02 expression system

(Table 1).


<!-- Page 15 -->


14

Using BL21(DE3) E. coli cells to express pCP-01 and pCP-02, a checkerboard assay was

performed by inoculating freshly transformed single colonies expressing the dioxygenase activity

(pCP-02) and not expressing the dioxygenase activity (pCP-01) in an alternating fashion in a 96-

well plate (Figure 10A).

This seed plate was then used the next morning to inoculate a fresh 96-well plate where the

cells were grown to exponential phase, followed by a media swap and resuspension in minimal

media according to the Marley method.35 After a short recovery period, the cultures were induced

with IPTG and fed with the aromatic substrate, toluene. The Marley method transfers cells into

fresh minimal growth media before inducing the cells to insure increase protein expression by the

removal of cytotoxic products that can arise from the over growth of cells, which can inhibit

protein expression.35 The procedure is also essential for the growth of cultures expressing Rieske

dioxygenases, as these enzymes are known to metabolize the tryptophan present in rich medias

into indigo, which is toxic to the cells.35, 36 After an incubation period with the substrate, cultures

*Table 1: Percent increase of metabolite production from pCDF-Duet (pCP-02) over the existing system (pDTG601A).*


<!-- Page 16 -->

were pelleted and 100 µL of supernatant was transferred to a new 96-well black opaque plate and

treated under the MPFCD conditions.31 Strong fluorescence signals were observed for wells

containing the cultures expressing toluene dioxygenase (E. coli BL21 (DE3) pCP-02) over the

wells with the culture lacking the catalytic oxidase subunit (E. coli BL21 (DE3) pCP-01) (Figure

10B). This assay clearly demonstrated the utility of the MPFCD system for the detection of cis-

diol metabolites produced by respiring cells.

The statistical effect size (Z’) has been used to evaluate assay systems as a means to

determine whether or not the statistical difference between two samples was sufficiently

significant to validate the assay system.37 The Z-factor between the cultures expressing TDO and

the cultures not expressing the oxygenase subunit was 0.78, indicating a statistically significant

fluorescence increase from cultures expressing for TDO.

Application of the MPFCD Assay

Having developed a robust screening platform capable of detecting the relative activity of

cultures expressing Rieske dioxygenases, it was determined to use this assay system to detect the

activity of the parent enzyme for a small library of aromatic substrates. These substrate scope

studies are often employed by synthetic chemists to determine the suitability of Rieske

dioxygenases for a given synthetic sequence, and typically involve several small-scale

*Figure 10: A) Scheme demonstrating the procedure for the whole-cell checkerboard assay; B) Fluorescence response of checkerboard assay with and without cultures expressing toluene dioxygenase (n = 30). Data normalized to the mean fluorescence response of cultures not expressing toluene dioxygenase ([I – I0] / I0)), the statistical effect size (Z’) for this assay was calculated as 0.78.*


<!-- Page 17 -->


16

fermentations, metabolite extractions and analysis.18 With our assay’s ability to simultaneously

detect the activity of many cultures, it was recognized to have the potential to significantly expedite

such studies. These substrates studies were conducted on toluene dioxygenase using the novel

pCP-02 plasmid in E. coli BL21 (DE3) and the novel pCP-01 plasmid in E. coli BL21 (DE3) as

the negative control. A range of aromatic substrates were tested to assess the utility of our assay

system in this context.31

Optimal fit studies of the active site of toluene dioxygenase have shown the likelihood of

alkyl groups larger than propyl, showing less success of undergoing dihydroxylation.38, 39 This was

seen in our substrate scope study, which demonstrated decreased fluorescence responses with

increased alkyl substituent size (Figure 11A). The docking site for the substrate in the active site

is aided by nonpolar amino acids, the majority of them being hydrophobic.38 This explains why

highly polar substrates such as phenethylamine and benzamide showed no fluorescent response

(Figure 11B).

The results of this study, being consistent with the established substrate scope of toluene

dioxygenase, confirmed the utility of the MPFCD assay in this context. Having established this

utility, we determined to perform saturation mutagenesis on targeted residues in the active site of

TDO to produce rationally generated libraries of TDO variants and to screen the variant libraries

for their dihydroxylation activity using the MPFCD assay.

Targeted Mutagenesis of todC2

The primary goal of the development of the MPFCD assay system is to apply it as a simple

and high throughput screening method that can be used to detect the relative activity of Rieske

dioxygenase variants produced through mutagenesis. With the availability of the X-ray structure

of toluene dioxygenase (Figure 12), residues in the active site of the enzyme (todC1) and in close

proximity to the substituent on the aromatic substrate were chosen for saturation mutagenesis.11

The Leucine-272 residue was the first selected for saturated mutagenesis using the ‘NNK’ protocol

via PCR.40

The active site mutation from leucine to proline was shown to terminate the activity of the

enzyme for the parent substrate toluene, while the mutation from leucine to phenylalanine was

shown to retain approximately parent levels of activity and the mutation from leucine to valine

was shown to decrease the activity of the enzyme for the parent substrate. To determine whether

these mutations altered the selectivity of the enzyme, the isolated variants L272V and L272F were

subjected to the substrate scope assay protocol as previously described.

The mutation from leucine to phenylalanine was shown not to affect the selectivity of the

enzyme (Figure 14), while the mutation from leucine to valine was shown to significantly alter

the selectivity of the enzyme (Figure 15).

*Figure 14: A) Aromatic substrates used in mutant studies. B) Toluene dioxygenase L272F mutant substrate scope. Mutants analyzed using the designed assay system (n = 4 for each substrate). Fluorescence responses normalized to negative control ([I – I0] / I0)).*

This mutation in the active site altered the selectivity of the enzyme to favor larger

substrates over the native substrate (toluene) and abolished the activity of the enzyme for benzyl

alcohol (Figure 15). The toluene dioxygenase active site is broken up into four pockets, with L272

being located in the most hydrophobic pocket.38 Smaller, less bulkier substrates, interact in this

pocket to maximize lipophilic interactions with minimal steric hinderances.38 The mutation from

a longer hydrophobic chain, leucine, to a shorter hydrophobic chain, valine, can aid in the

interactions of a larger substrate to be metabolized in the active site of TDO. This was the first

study to identify L272 as playing a major role in the selectivity of toluene dioxygenase.

## Conclusions

Here, a novel, robust, and high-throughput fluorescence-based assay system has been

developed to detect the cis-diol metabolites produced by Rieske dioxygenases. The MPFCD assay

was optimized to determine the optimal assay conditions that maximize the sensitivity of the

system. This assay system was shown to be capable of detecting very low concentrations of cis-

diol metabolites (below 10 µM) by using HEPES buffer (a non-coordinating buffer system), and

creating a slightly acidic environment to promote imine formation (aldehyde-probe conjugation).

The four enzyme components of toluene dioxygenase system were cloned into a new, modern

*Figure 15: A) Aromatic substrates tested with L272V mutants. B) Relative fluorescence response of native enzyme compared to mutant. Data normalized by using negative control, (E. coli BL21 (DE3) pCP-01).*


<!-- Page 23 -->


22

expression vector, pCP-02, that has been used in these studies as a template for mutagenesis, as a

positive control and to determine the activity of the parent enzyme. The utility of the MPFCD

assay system in evaluating the substrate scope of Rieske dioxygenases was confirmed. The

MPFCD system has also been shown to effectively detect the relative metabolite production of

Rieske dioxygenase variant libraries. The ability of the MPFCD assay to perform the facile

determination of the effect of mutations on the activity and selectivity of the Rieske dioxygenases

has also been demonstrated. The utility of the assay system in this context was demonstrated by

producing a library of toluene dioxygenase mutants through saturation mutagenesis and screening

this variant library for the dihydroxylation activity of the library members. This initial screening

assay also identified a toluene dioxygenase variant with significantly altered reactivity, L272V.

These results demonstrate not only the applicability of the assay system in screening large enzyme

variant libraries but also in identifying enzyme variants with significantly altered reactivity.

The increasing need to create environmentally friendly alternatives to typical chemical

processes highlighted the potential for the use of enzymes in synthetic chemistry.42, 43 Here, a new

assay system was developed to screen for improved Rieske dioxygenase variants which can be

used as green chemical tools for the chemical community by mitigating or eliminating the need

for petroleum based solvents and toxic metal catalysts. Novel Rieske dioxygenase variants

produced and identified through our directed evolution platform have shown the potential for

expanded reactivity over the parent enzyme. Application of the metabolites produced by these

novel variants as chiral building blocks for making high value compounds have the potential to

decrease the environmental impact of the chemical industry.

Experimental Section

Materials

Primers for saturated mutagenesis were designed with QuikChangeÒ primer design tool

from Agilent Technologies. PCR was performed on an ABI GeneAmpÒ 9700 Thermal Cycler.

QuikChangeÒ XL II kit from Agilent technologies was used for saturated mutagenesis. E. coli

JM109 (pDTG601A)15 was kindly donated from Professor David Gibson (1938-2014) and

Professor Rebeca Parales from University of California, Davis. E. coli JM109 and BL21 (DE3)

competent cells were obtained from Agilent Technologies and Thermofisher respectively. Plasmid

isolation was performed using New England BioLabs MonarchÒ miniprep kit. Transformations

were performed using an Eppendorf EporatorÒ. SOC growth medium for recovery of

transformations, was made following a Cold Springs Harbor Protocol.44 Luria broth, agar, IPTG

were all obtained from RPI (Research Products International). All other reagents were obtained

from MilliporeSigma. Growth media and buffers were all adjusted to a pH of 7.2 using NaOH.

Streptomycin or ampicillin were added to growth media at 100 and 50 µg/mL respectively. A

sterile environment was made by wiping down surfaces with 95% ethanol and working under a

butane flame. Whole cell assay cultures were grown by picking single colonies with sterile

toothpicks into clear, polystyrene, Greiner Bio-One, 96-well plates. MPFCD fluorescence assays

were performed using Corningâ polystyrene black, opaque flat bottom 96-well plates.

Fluorescence analyses was performed on a BioTekâ SynergyTM H1 monochromator-based multi-

mode plate reader using Gen5 3.08 software. E. coli culture and plates were grown at 37 oC and

assay plates were grown at 30 oC after induction. All MPFCD reactions were performed at room

temperature.

96-well Plate Fermentation

Isolated plasmids of pCP-01, pCP-02 and TDO mutant library were transformed into E.

coli BL21 (BE3) electrocompetent cells using an electroporator and left to recover in SOC media

for one hour at 37 oC in a shaking incubator. The cultures were plated on LB + agar with

streptomycin and grown at 37 oC overnight. The next day, single colonies were picked with sterile

toothpicks into a 96-well round bottom plate with 160 µL of LB + streptomycin and 0.3% glucose.

These seed plates were incubated with shaking at 37 oC overnight. 5 µL of the seed plate wells

were used to inoculate a new 96-well round bottom plate containing 155 µL of LB + streptomycin.

These plates were grown in a shaking incubator for 2.5 hours at 37 oC. These assay plates were

than pelleted on a Thermo Sorvall Legend XTR Refrigerated Centrifuge at 3500 rpm for 10 mins

at 4 oC. The cells were resuspended in minimal media (see recipe above) containing streptomycin

and incubated for one hour with shaking at 37 oC. Assay plates were then induced with 5 µL of

IPTG stock solution to a final concentration 0.5 mM was done. Temperature was reduced to 30 oC

and plates were shaken for two hours. Following the induction period, 5 µL of aromatic substrate

stock solutions in DMSO were added to assay plates to a final concentration of 2 mM. After one

hour of incubation at 30 oC, the cultures were pelleted. 100 µL of the supernatant was transferred

methanol + concentrated HCl (3 µL/mL) was added to the plates for a final concentration of 0.1
